options: Try to obtain records, but do not accept parental recall alone; if documentation remains inadequate, consider the child unimmunized and start an age- and risk-appropriate schedule
Accept the parent's recollection as proof and give no further vaccines
Order broad serologic testing for every vaccine before giving any dose
Wait until school entry before deciding whether vaccination is needed
Refuse vaccination because prior doses might have been given elsewhere
rationale: Canadian guidance says to attempt to obtain previous records. For children, parental recall without vaccine-provider documentation should not be accepted as evidence of immunization. When adequate documentation cannot be obtained, consider the child unimmunized and begin the schedule appropriate for age and risk factors; routine broad serology is generally not practical.

text: An 8-year-old newly arrived in Canada brings a written vaccine record. The documented doses were given at ages and intervals compatible with the Canadian schedule. What is the best next step?
options: Accept the valid documented doses, compare them with the Canadian schedule, and give only doses still needed
Discard every overseas record and automatically restart all series
Ignore the dates because country of origin never matters
Assume every written record is invalid without reviewing it
Give no vaccines or follow-up because the child has a written card
rationale: Vaccination from another country can be counted when there is written documentation and the ages and intervals are comparable with the Canadian schedule. The clinician should review the record and provide only additional doses that are required. Automatic repetition or automatic acceptance without review are both shortcuts.

text: A 22-year-old has laboratory-confirmed urogenital gonorrhea. Their most recent sexual partner, 38 days ago, has no symptoms. Which partner plan is most appropriate?
options: Notify, clinically assess, test and empirically treat sexual partners from the prior 60 days without waiting for their test results
Treat partners only if they develop symptoms
Wait for every partner's test result before offering treatment
Notify only partners from the previous seven days
Provide no partner care once the index patient receives treatment
rationale: Canadian gonorrhea guidance recommends notification, clinical assessment, testing and empiric treatment for sexual partners in the 60 days before symptom onset or specimen collection. Treatment is recommended regardless of clinical findings and should not wait for test results.

text: A patient and their current partner both receive a single-dose gonorrhea treatment today. When can they resume sexual activity without barrier protection?
options: After seven days have passed after single-dose therapy and symptoms have resolved
Immediately after the injections are given
After 24 hours even if symptoms persist
Only after a year of abstinence
Whenever one partner feels well, regardless of the other partner's treatment
rationale: People diagnosed with gonorrhea and their partners should avoid sexual activity without barrier protection until treatment for the person and all current partners is complete and symptoms have resolved. After single-dose therapy, the recommended interval is seven days.

text: A primary-care clinic plans to administer a depression questionnaire with a fixed cut-off score to every adult who has no symptoms or clinical suspicion of depression. What does the 2025 Canadian Task Force recommendation advise?
options: Do not routinely screen every adult with a questionnaire and cut-off score solely to label people screen-positive or screen-negative
Use the questionnaire at every visit for all adults without exception
Do not assess depression in any patient who reports symptoms
Screen only people older than 75 years regardless of symptoms
Replace clinical assessment with a single questionnaire score
rationale: The Canadian Task Force recommends against routine instrument-based screening of all adults using a questionnaire cut-off. This does not apply to people with symptoms, a current diagnosis, or clinical suspicion of a mental health disorder, who need clinical assessment.

text: A 63-year-old at average risk for colorectal cancer has no bowel symptoms and asks about screening. Which option is consistent with Canadian Task Force guidance?
options: Fecal occult blood testing, including FIT, every two years or flexible sigmoidoscopy every 10 years
Screening colonoscopy every year for every average-risk adult
Tumour-marker blood testing as the only screening test
rationale: For average-risk adults aged 50 to 74, the Canadian Task Force recommends stool-based fecal occult blood testing every two years or flexible sigmoidoscopy every 10 years. FIT can be used in place of guaiac testing because of its greater sensitivity with similar specificity.

sub: Age limit for average-risk colorectal screening
text: A healthy 78-year-old at average risk for colorectal cancer has no symptoms and no previous abnormal screening. What is the Canadian Task Force recommendation for routine screening?
options: Do not routinely screen average-risk adults aged 75 years and older
Begin annual colonoscopy because risk rises with age
Order a CT abdomen every year
Use a stool test every month
Screen only if a family member requests it
rationale: The Canadian Task Force recommends against routine colorectal screening in average-risk adults aged 75 years and older. This screening recommendation does not replace diagnostic work-up of new symptoms.

text: A community-dwelling 68-year-old woman is not taking preventive pharmacotherapy for fragility fractures and asks about screening. According to the Canadian Task Force guideline, what is the best first step?
options: Use Canadian clinical FRAX without BMD, then use her 10-year major osteoporotic fracture risk for shared decision-making
Order BMD alone before any risk assessment or discussion
Start preventive pharmacotherapy without estimating risk
Avoid all assessment because no fracture has occurred
Use a routine screening pathway intended for men
rationale: For eligible women aged 65 years or older, the guideline recommends a risk-assessment-first approach: Canadian clinical FRAX without BMD, followed by shared decision-making using the 10-year major osteoporotic fracture risk.

sub: When to add BMD to FRAX
text: An eligible 69-year-old woman has completed Canadian clinical FRAX without BMD. After discussing the result, she is considering preventive pharmacotherapy. What is the best next step?
options: Request femoral-neck DXA, then re-estimate fracture risk by adding the BMD T-score to FRAX
Repeat the same clinical FRAX every month without further discussion
Start medication without considering her risk estimate or preference
Order spinal imaging instead of BMD for all screening decisions
Stop the assessment because FRAX can never be updated
rationale: If preventive pharmacotherapy is being considered after the risk discussion, the guideline advises femoral-neck BMD measurement by DXA and recalculation of FRAX using the BMD T-score.

text: A community-dwelling 71-year-old man has no fragility fracture and is not taking preventive pharmacotherapy. According to the Canadian Task Force screening guideline, what is the best statement?
options: It recommends against routine primary-prevention screening in males aged 40 years or older
It recommends BMD-first screening for every man aged 40 years or older
It recommends preventive medication for every man regardless of risk
It recommends no attention to new risk factors or secondary prevention
It recommends using a screening pathway only after an acute fracture
rationale: For primary prevention, this Task Force guideline recommends against screening males aged 40 years or older because benefit was not established. This does not remove the need to assess new risk factors or manage secondary prevention after a fracture.

text: A community-dwelling 57-year-old woman is not taking preventive pharmacotherapy and has no fragility fracture. Which statement reflects the Canadian Task Force screening recommendation?
options: Routine primary-prevention screening is recommended against for females aged 40 to 64 years
All women should have BMD testing every year from age 40
Preventive medication should begin without a risk discussion
A screening guideline means clinicians should ignore new clinical risk factors
Only men should be assessed for fragility-fracture risk
rationale: The Task Force recommends against routine screening of females aged 40 to 64 years for primary prevention of fragility fractures. The scope is community-dwelling people not currently on preventive pharmacotherapy and does not replace clinical assessment when circumstances change.

text: A 66-year-old woman previously completed an eligible fracture-risk assessment and follow-up BMD testing three years ago. She has no new risk factor, fracture, or major change in health. What is the best advice about routine rescreening?
options: Routine rescreening within eight years does not appear useful when no clinical change has occurred
Repeat BMD every year for all eligible women
Repeat BMD every three months to improve FRAX accuracy
Start preventive medication solely because three years have passed
Never reconsider fracture risk even if a fragility fracture or major risk change occurs
rationale: The guideline found that repeating BMD at intervals of three to eight years did not improve fracture-risk prediction; rescreening within eight years does not appear useful. New risk factors or a fragility fracture still require clinical reassessment.

text: Which group of resources should be prioritized first when verifying MCCQE1 clinical management decisions in the user-provided source list?
options: BC Guidelines, Alberta Guidelines, RxFiles, Bugs and Drugs, Do Bugs Need Drugs, Choosing Wisely Canada, CEP, MQ6 and Alberta Antenatal Pathway
Only non-Canadian blogs because they are easier to read
Only image-based dermatology sites for every specialty
Only patient leaflets without clinician guidelines
Only broad encyclopedias without Canadian context
rationale: Prioritize Canadian and provincial guidance first. Core sources from the file include RxFiles, Bugs and Drugs, Do Bugs Need Drugs, Alberta Diabetes Link, CEP, Alberta/BC Guidelines, Choosing Wisely Canada, medSask minor ailment guidance, Specialist Link, MQ6 and the Alberta Antenatal Pathway. Use them to anchor management, stewardship, counselling and referral decisions.

text: A student wants to strengthen MCCQE1 questions that ask “What should you say next?” or “What is the best counselling response?” Which sources from the list match best?
options: UBC 99 Priority Topics, CMPA, Choosing Wisely Canada, TheNNT, This Changed My Practice and Do Bugs Need Drugs
Orthobullets and foot surgery pages only
rationale: Communication and ethics are best supported by UBC priority topics such as Bad News, Counselling, Difficult Patient, Domestic Violence, Mental Competency and Violent/Aggressive Patient. CMPA supports consent, disclosure and documentation. Choosing Wisely and TheNNT support risk-benefit communication. Do Bugs Need Drugs supports antibiotic refusal and safety-netting.

sub: Dermatology, orthopedics and physical exam sources
text: Which sources from the uploaded list are useful as clinical recognition or examination aids rather than primary Canadian management guidelines?
options: DermNet, Skinsight, Skin Therapy Letter, Orthobullets, Stanford Medicine 25, UCSD Clinical Medicine, NYU neurosurgery modules and Edmonton Bone and Joint
rationale: DermNet, Skinsight and Skin Therapy Letter are strong for dermatology pattern recognition and counselling. Orthobullets, Stanford Medicine 25, UCSD Clinical Medicine, NYU modules and Edmonton Bone and Joint help anatomy, examination and orthopedic reasoning. They are helpful, but Canadian guideline sources should still verify management when a Canadian recommendation exists.

text: Which source group is best used for patient-facing counselling language and safety-netting examples?
options: Fraser Health patient education, BC Diabetes handouts, BAD patient information leaflets, FootCareMD, OrthoInfo, AAFP handouts, Cirrhosis Care and Do Bugs Need Drugs viral prescription pad
rationale: Patient handouts help you phrase explanations in plain language. They are useful for MCCQE1 communication, teach-back and safety-net questions. They should not replace clinician guidelines for diagnosis or treatment thresholds.

text: Which listed sources are best treated as useful specialty support rather than first-line MCCQE1 core sources?
options: Merck Manual Professional, FPNotebook, OpenEvidence, DigitalDDx, FMLearner, Time of Care, The Hub UofT Family, Specialist Link, eFrailty and pricingdoc ACFP
BC Guidelines and Alberta Guidelines only
rationale: These sources can be helpful for differential diagnosis, quick review, teaching cases, referral pathways, frailty assessment and Alberta drug cost context. Use them after core Canadian guidance, or when the core source does not cover the point being tested.

text: A patient has recovered after emergency treatment of an opioid overdose. Which harm-reduction intervention should be included in discharge planning?
options: Advise the patient to avoid being alone but provide no medication
Provide access to a take-home naloxone kit and teach overdose recognition and response
Recommend activated charcoal for any future overdose
Explain that naloxone requires a prescription in Canada
rationale: Health Canada states that take-home naloxone is available without a prescription at most pharmacies and local health authorities. People at risk of overdose, and people likely to witness one, should have access to a kit and know how to recognize an overdose, call emergency services, administer naloxone, support breathing, and repeat naloxone every 2 to 3 minutes when needed. Naloxone is temporary and does not replace emergency assessment.

text: A 49-year-old has a persistent firm, enlarging palpable breast mass with skin dimpling. A screening mammogram three months ago was reported as negative. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Arrange prompt diagnostic breast assessment rather than reassure on the basis of the negative screening mammogram
Return to routine screening in two years with no further assessment
Assume the mass is benign because the screening study was negative
Give antibiotics alone and defer breast assessment unless fever develops
Advise self-examination only and no clinician follow-up
rationale: A screening mammogram is not a complete diagnostic assessment of a persistent symptomatic breast finding. Alberta guidance notes that a breast mass not seen on mammography may need additional diagnostic work-up. The correct next decision is prompt assessment, not reassurance based on a screening result.

text: A 54-year-old has a standardized office blood pressure of 152/94 mm Hg at the first visit, with no hypertensive emergency features. What is the preferred next diagnostic approach?
options: Confirm with ambulatory blood pressure monitoring; use home monitoring if ambulatory monitoring is not tolerated, available, or preferred
Diagnose hypertension from one routine office reading and never repeat it
Start a three-drug regimen without further assessment
Ignore the result until symptoms develop
Use only a wrist monitor reading from the waiting room
rationale: When an initial office measurement is elevated but below the threshold that establishes hypertension immediately, out-of-office measurement should be used to confirm the diagnosis. ABPM is preferred, while HBPM is appropriate when ABPM is not feasible or acceptable.

text: A patient has repeated elevated office blood pressures but a properly performed home blood-pressure series is below the diagnostic threshold. There is no acute target-organ injury. What is the best interpretation and plan?
options: Consider white coat hypertension and do not begin antihypertensive medication solely on the elevated office readings
Diagnose resistant hypertension and add several medications
Treat the home readings as invalid because they are lower
Start medication only if the patient reports headache
rationale: When out-of-office measurements are not elevated, white coat hypertension should be considered. Pharmacotherapy should not be initiated solely because office readings are high; ongoing monitoring and cardiovascular risk assessment remain important.

text: At a first assessment, a patient has a mean standardized office blood pressure of 184/112 mm Hg. They have no chest pain, focal deficit, pulmonary edema, or other signs of acute target-organ injury. Which diagnostic principle is correct?
options: Hypertension can be diagnosed at this visit; assess for urgency or emergency and arrange appropriate management rather than waiting for routine out-of-office confirmation
The reading is normal because the patient feels well
Home monitoring must be completed before the clinician can recognize hypertension
The patient needs no follow-up unless blood pressure exceeds 250/150 mm Hg
A single elevated diastolic reading can never matter
rationale: Hypertension Canada states that a first-visit mean office systolic pressure of 180 mm Hg or diastolic pressure of 110 mm Hg establishes hypertension. The clinician must still assess for features of hypertensive urgency or emergency and manage accordingly.

text: A 58-year-old has confirmed hypertension with a blood pressure of 144/92 mm Hg. What treatment approach aligns with the 2025 Hypertension Canada primary-care guideline?
options: Begin pharmacotherapy together with healthy lifestyle changes
Use lifestyle changes only for several years before considering medication
Start medication but advise against lifestyle changes
Treat only if the patient develops a stroke
Avoid follow-up because the pressure is below 160/100 mm Hg
rationale: For adults with confirmed blood pressure of 140/90 mm Hg or higher, Hypertension Canada recommends pharmacotherapy along with healthy lifestyle changes. Medication complements rather than replaces lifestyle care.

sub: Hypertension treatment in high cardiovascular risk
text: A 72-year-old with diabetes has confirmed systolic blood pressure of 134 mm Hg on standardized measurements. What is the best management principle?
options: Use pharmacotherapy together with healthy lifestyle changes because systolic 130 to 139 mm Hg with high cardiovascular risk meets the treatment threshold
Provide reassurance because medication is never used below 140 mm Hg
Use a medication only after a hypertensive emergency occurs
Avoid lifestyle counselling because diabetes is already present
Treat solely according to the diastolic pressure
rationale: The 2025 guideline recommends pharmacotherapy for systolic pressure of 130 to 139 mm Hg in adults at high cardiovascular risk, including people with diabetes, in addition to lifestyle change.

text: A 42-year-old without diabetes, chronic kidney disease, established cardiovascular disease, or other high-risk features has confirmed systolic blood pressure of 134 mm Hg. What is the most appropriate initial plan?
options: Emphasize healthy lifestyle changes and reassess blood pressure within 3 to 6 months
Treat only if diastolic pressure reaches 120 mm Hg
Avoid exercise because it can raise blood pressure temporarily
rationale: For systolic pressure of 130 to 139 mm Hg in a person without high cardiovascular risk, Hypertension Canada advises lifestyle change and reassessment in 3 to 6 months. If the range persists and risk remains low, periodic reassessment continues.

text: A 63-year-old is being treated for confirmed hypertension and tolerates therapy without orthostasis, falls, or other limiting adverse effects. What systolic target is recommended by the 2025 Hypertension Canada guideline?
options: Below 130 mm Hg, provided treatment is well tolerated
Below 100 mm Hg for every patient
No target is needed once a medication is prescribed
Below 130/30 mm Hg regardless of symptoms
rationale: Healthy lifestyle changes with or without pharmacotherapy are recommended to achieve systolic blood pressure below 130 mm Hg when this is well tolerated. Frailty, falls, orthostatic symptoms, and goals of care can require individualized adjustment.

sub: Low back pain without red flags
text: A 40-year-old has two weeks of mechanical low back pain after lifting boxes. They have normal strength, sensation, reflexes, bowel and bladder function, and no fever, cancer history, infection risk, or trauma. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Provide conservative management and avoid routine early spinal imaging
Order urgent MRI solely because pain has lasted two weeks
Order CT of the whole spine before any examination
Schedule epidural steroid injection as first-line care
Advise complete bed rest until imaging is obtained
rationale: Choosing Wisely Canada advises against imaging for lower back pain unless red flags are present. In uncomplicated acute mechanical pain, conservative care and appropriate activity are preferred; early imaging can lead to unnecessary downstream intervention.

sub: Who is included in adult smoking-cessation care
text: A 29-year-old smokes commercial cigarettes only on some weekends and says they are not ready to quit. Which approach is most consistent with the Canadian adult smoking-cessation guideline?
options: Include them in cessation care: encourage stopping and offer one or more recommended interventions
Wait until they smoke every day before discussing cessation
Avoid cessation care until they state that they are motivated to quit
Offer support only if they have a smoking-related disease
Treat occasional smoking as traditional ceremonial tobacco use
rationale: The guideline applies to non-pregnant adults who currently smoke commercial cigarettes regularly or occasionally, whether or not they feel ready to quit. Clinicians should encourage cessation and offer at least one recommended intervention.

text: A 54-year-old who smokes cigarettes attends for a routine visit and has not raised smoking. What is the best clinician action?
options: Know the patient’s smoking status, encourage stopping, and offer one or more recommended cessation interventions
Avoid the topic unless the patient specifically requests medication
Give cessation counselling only after spirometry is abnormal
Refer for an alternative therapy before discussing evidence-based options
Document smoking only when tobacco use is the presenting complaint
rationale: Smoking status is part of good clinical care. Adults who smoke should be encouraged to stop and offered one or more recommended cessation interventions; waiting for a disease complication or a request misses an opportunity for prevention.

text: A patient who smokes asks, “Which single quit method do you always prescribe?” What is the best response?
options: Review the recommended options and choose together based on evidence, values, preferences, and practical fit
Insist on one medication because it is the only acceptable first-line choice
Tell the patient to choose an option without clinician input
Defer all discussion until a future visit because several options exist
Recommend an unproven alternative before discussing behavioural or pharmacologic support
rationale: The guideline calls for shared decision-making. A clinician should help the patient compare recommended behavioural, pharmacologic, or combined options and make a choice that fits the person’s preferences and circumstances.

text: A patient wants a non-drug option to help stop smoking. Which option belongs on the recommended behavioural menu?
options: Advice or education from a healthcare provider, with counselling, text-message support, or self-help materials as other options
Hypnotherapy as the preferred evidence-based intervention
Laser therapy to the ear as the routine first choice
St. John’s wort without any cessation support
Continuous auricular stimulation as the standard behavioural treatment
rationale: Recommended behavioural interventions include provider advice or education, trained individual or group counselling, mobile text-message interventions, and self-help materials. The guideline recommends against several alternative interventions, including hypnotherapy, laser therapy, and continuous auricular stimulation.

text: A non-pregnant adult wants medication support for cigarette cessation and has no contraindication to the listed options. Which set is included in the Canadian guideline’s recommended pharmacotherapy choices?
options: Nicotine replacement therapy, varenicline, bupropion, and cytisine
No pharmacotherapy can be considered until behavioural treatment has failed
rationale: The recommended pharmacotherapy options are nicotine replacement therapy, varenicline, bupropion, and cytisine. The appropriate individual choice still depends on contraindications, adverse effects, access, and patient preference.

text: A patient has relapsed after trying to quit with self-help materials alone. They are open to a more intensive plan and have no contraindication to medication. Which plan is best supported?
options: Offer a combined behavioural and pharmacotherapy approach through shared decision-making
Repeat self-help alone and avoid discussing medication or counselling
Recommend an e-cigarette as the routine first escalation for every patient
Use hypnotherapy instead of evidence-based care
Wait until the patient develops tobacco-related disease
rationale: Combined behavioural and pharmacotherapy approaches are recommended options. After a relapse, reassess barriers and preferences, then offer effective support rather than treating relapse as a reason to stop helping.

text: A patient lives far from an in-person program and asks whether an interactive online quit program can be used. Which option is most consistent with the guideline?
options: It may be considered when it includes additional behavioural support
It should replace all clinician contact and behavioural support
It is recommended only if the patient continues smoking
It is a reason to avoid discussing other recommended options
It is equivalent to an unproven alternative therapy
rationale: An interactive computer-based or online program with additional behavioural support may be considered. The added support is the key distinction from a stand-alone app or website.

text: A patient plans to use only an interactive quit-smoking app, with no counselling, clinician contact, text support, or other behavioural support. What is the best advice?
options: Do not rely on the stand-alone app alone; offer additional behavioural support or another recommended option
A stand-alone app is the strongly preferred intervention for every patient
The app removes the need to ask about smoking status
The app is appropriate only when used with an unproven alternative therapy
No cessation intervention should be offered until the app fails
rationale: The guideline suggests against interactive online programs that involve only the individual and a website or app, without additional behavioural support. Discuss a supported online program or other recommended interventions instead.

text: A 44-year-old who smokes asks to start an e-cigarette as their first and only quit strategy. They have not tried other cessation supports and do not express a strong preference for e-cigarettes. What is the best next step?
options: Discuss recommended behavioural, pharmacotherapy, and combined options rather than using e-cigarettes as routine first treatment
Prescribe an e-cigarette as the standard first-line option for all people who smoke
Tell the patient to continue smoking until an e-cigarette is approved
Recommend e-cigarettes without explaining any uncertainty
Offer no cessation support because the patient mentioned vaping
rationale: The guideline suggests against e-cigarettes for most people seeking cessation. Standard recommended options should be reviewed first; e-cigarettes may be discussed in specific circumstances through shared decision-making.

text: A patient has unsuccessfully attempted recommended cessation interventions and now strongly prefers an e-cigarette to help stop smoking. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Use shared decision-making to discuss possible e-cigarette use, including its limits and uncertainties
State that e-cigarettes are required after any failed quit attempt
Refuse to discuss cessation further because prior attempts failed
Describe e-cigarettes as having established long-term safety
Recommend an alternative therapy instead of discussing evidence-based options
rationale: For people who have unsuccessfully tried other interventions, are unwilling to try them, or strongly prefer e-cigarettes, clinicians may use shared decision-making to discuss possible use. This is an exception to the general suggestion against e-cigarettes for cessation.

text: After shared decision-making, a patient elects to try a nicotine-containing e-cigarette to stop smoking. Which counselling point is essential?
options: Long-term safety data are lacking, approved therapeutic products with consistent formulations are unavailable, and nicotine addiction may continue
The product has proven long-term safety and eliminates nicotine addiction
The formulation is standardized as an approved cessation medicine
No discussion is needed because the patient chose it
Using an e-cigarette guarantees permanent smoking cessation
rationale: People who decide to use e-cigarettes for cessation should be informed that approved therapeutic products with consistent formulations are lacking, long-term safety data are unavailable, and nicotine use can continue.

sub: Routine cognitive screening in asymptomatic older adults
text: A healthy 73-year-old reports no memory concern, manages finances and medications independently, and has no family or clinician concern about cognition. They ask whether they should have a routine MoCA solely because of age. What is the best response?
options: Do not routinely perform instrument-based cognitive screening in an asymptomatic older adult
Perform annual cognitive testing for every adult aged 65 or older
Order brain imaging before discussing symptoms or function
Start a cognitive medication before assessing concern
Ask a family member to consent to screening instead
rationale: The Canadian Task Force recommends against instrument-based screening for cognitive impairment in asymptomatic adults aged 65 years or older. This is a screening recommendation, not a reason to ignore new concerns or symptoms.

text: A 70-year-old reports six months of worsening word-finding and difficulty following familiar recipes. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Undertake a clinical assessment of the cognitive concern rather than treating this as routine asymptomatic screening
Reassure the patient that cognitive testing is never appropriate after age 65
Decline assessment because the guideline recommends against universal screening
Wait for a family member to report a problem before evaluating
rationale: The recommendation against screening does not apply when the patient raises cognitive concerns or has symptoms suggesting cognitive impairment. New cognitive symptoms need an appropriate clinical assessment.

text: A 76-year-old denies difficulties, but their daughter reports repeated missed bills and new trouble finding words. What is the best interpretation of the preventive guideline?
options: This is not asymptomatic screening; caregiver concern warrants clinical assessment
No assessment is needed because the patient personally denies symptoms
Routine screening is prohibited for all older adults
The daughter should complete an online quiz instead of seeking care
A cognitive medication should be started without assessment
rationale: The guideline explicitly excludes people suspected of cognitive impairment by family, friends, caregivers, or clinicians from its recommendation against routine screening. Collateral concern and functional change should prompt clinical assessment.

text: An 81-year-old has recently begun missing medication doses and getting lost on a route used for years. Which approach is best?
options: Arrange clinical assessment of possible cognitive impairment; do not dismiss functional change using a no-screening recommendation
Avoid any cognitive evaluation because the person is older than 65
Repeat a screening questionnaire yearly without further assessment
Assume normal aging and make no plan
Start treatment for dementia without evaluating the change
rationale: Changes in day-to-day function can be suggestive of cognitive impairment or dementia. The recommendation against instrument-based screening applies only to asymptomatic adults and does not replace assessment of symptoms or functional decline.

text: A 66-year-old had 25 minutes of aphasia and right arm weakness this morning. Symptoms have fully resolved. The examination is normal in the emergency department. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Arrange urgent brain imaging with concurrent neurovascular imaging through a stroke pathway before emergency-department discharge
Reassure and arrange routine outpatient follow-up in several weeks
Order only an EEG because the symptoms resolved
Wait for a second event before investigating
rationale: A transient focal neurologic deficit is a possible TIA or non-disabling stroke. Canadian Stroke Best Practices recommend urgent brain imaging with concurrent neurovascular imaging as soon as possible and before emergency-department discharge.

text: A patient with suspected high-risk TIA needs acute vascular assessment. Which imaging strategy is first-line when available and appropriate?
options: CT angiography of the head and neck, alongside urgent brain imaging
Carotid massage in the emergency department
A screening echocardiogram as the only urgent study
Routine EEG before any vascular assessment
No imaging if the neurologic examination is normal
rationale: Canadian Stroke Best Practices identify CT angiography as the first-line vascular imaging test for stroke or TIA. If CTA is not possible, MRA or carotid ultrasound can be reasonable alternatives based on availability and patient factors.

text: A patient with non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke did not receive intravenous thrombolysis. Brain imaging has excluded hemorrhage. What is the best antithrombotic timing principle?
options: Start antiplatelet therapy as soon as possible, within 24 hours of symptom onset and ideally within 12 hours
Wait one week before any antithrombotic treatment
Start antiplatelet therapy before brain imaging
Use long-term dual antiplatelet therapy for every ischemic stroke
Avoid all secondary prevention after the first event
rationale: For ischemic stroke or TIA, antiplatelet therapy should start promptly after brain imaging excludes hemorrhage, unless there is another indication for anticoagulation or a treatment sequence that changes timing.

text: A patient received intravenous thrombolysis for acute ischemic stroke. When should routine antiplatelet therapy be reconsidered?
options: After the first 24 hours, once follow-up brain imaging has excluded secondary hemorrhage
Only after three months regardless of follow-up imaging
Never, because thrombolysis permanently replaces antiplatelet therapy
rationale: Canadian Stroke Best Practices advise avoiding antiplatelet therapy during the first 24 hours after intravenous thrombolysis. It can then be started after follow-up imaging has excluded secondary hemorrhage.

text: A patient has a high-risk TIA of non-cardioembolic origin, no high bleeding risk, and no reason for anticoagulation. Which secondary prevention regimen is recommended?
options: Clopidogrel plus acetylsalicylic acid for 21 days, then antiplatelet monotherapy
Dual antiplatelet therapy indefinitely for life
No antiplatelet treatment because symptoms resolved
Warfarin for every TIA regardless of mechanism
A single dose of aspirin only, with no ongoing plan
rationale: For acute high-risk TIA or minor non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke in people without high bleeding risk, Canadian Stroke Best Practices recommend clopidogrel plus acetylsalicylic acid for 21 days, followed by antiplatelet monotherapy. Longer routine dual therapy increases bleeding risk without clear benefit.

sub: AF after ischemic stroke or TIA
text: A patient with ischemic stroke is found to have AF and has no contraindication to anticoagulation. Which long-term antithrombotic strategy is recommended?
options: Oral anticoagulation rather than aspirin or dual antiplatelet therapy
Aspirin only because stroke already occurred
Dual antiplatelet therapy instead of anticoagulation
No therapy if AF is intermittent
Warfarin plus aspirin for every patient
rationale: For ischemic stroke or TIA associated with AF, oral anticoagulation is strongly recommended and is more effective than aspirin or dual antiplatelet therapy for secondary prevention.

text: A patient is being investigated for acute embolic ischemic stroke and could receive anticoagulation if AF is found. What rhythm monitoring is recommended in the initial work-up?
options: ECG monitoring for 24 hours or more
No cardiac testing if the admission ECG is normal
rationale: Because paroxysmal AF can be missed on a single ECG, at least 24 hours of ECG monitoring is recommended during the initial embolic stroke or TIA work-up when the result would change therapy.

text: A 61-year-old has an embolic stroke of undetermined source. Initial short-term ECG monitoring shows no AF, but a cardioembolic cause remains suspected and anticoagulation would be feasible. What is the best next test?
options: Prolonged ECG monitoring for at least two weeks
rationale: Selected patients aged 55 or older with suspected cardioembolic stroke or TIA and negative initial monitoring should receive prolonged ECG monitoring for at least two weeks to improve detection of paroxysmal AF.

text: A patient with AF has an ischemic stroke while prescribed a DOAC. What is the best next approach after acute stabilization?
options: Assume every DOAC has failed and add aspirin automatically
Switch blindly to warfarin without review
Check adherence, dose and renal appropriateness, interactions, competing stroke causes, and vascular risk factors
rationale: Stroke on anticoagulation requires a structured review of adherence, correct dosing, renal function, drug interactions, alternative stroke mechanisms, and vascular risk-factor control rather than automatic combination therapy.

text: A patient with an actively bleeding luminal gastrointestinal cancer develops a proximal DVT and can receive anticoagulation. Which agent is generally preferred when treatment starts?
options: No anticoagulant because cancer is present
A direct oral anticoagulant regardless of bleeding site
rationale: LMWH or selected anti-Xa DOACs can treat cancer-associated thrombosis, but LMWH is generally preferred when gastrointestinal or genitourinary bleeding risk is high.

text: A patient taking dabigatran for prior PE presents with life-threatening intracranial bleeding and clinically significant drug effect. Which specific reversal agent is indicated?
options: Tranexamic acid as the specific antidote
rationale: Idarucizumab is the specific reversal agent for life-threatening or uncontrolled bleeding due to dabigatran. Stabilization, source control, laboratory assessment, and supportive care occur in parallel.

text: A 72-year-old has episodic palpitations. ECG shows an irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm with no consistent P waves. What is the most likely diagnosis?
rationale: Atrial fibrillation is characterized by disorganized atrial activity, absent consistent P waves, and an irregularly irregular ventricular response.

text: A patient with AF and a ventricular rate of 170/min has hypotension, pulmonary edema, and ongoing ischemic chest pain attributable to the arrhythmia. What is the best immediate rhythm treatment?
options: Unsynchronized defibrillation while a pulse is present
rationale: Acute AF causing hemodynamic instability requires synchronized electrical cardioversion. Synchronization reduces the risk of delivering a shock during ventricular repolarization.

text: A stable patient has newly detected AF. Which initial approach best complements rate or rhythm treatment?
options: Order coronary angiography for every patient
Assess for contributors such as thyroid disease, infection, alcohol exposure, ischemia, heart failure, and electrolyte disturbance
Begin lifelong amiodarone before history or examination
Ignore comorbid disease until cardioversion fails
rationale: New AF warrants clinical assessment for reversible or aggravating contributors and structural heart disease while symptoms, rate, rhythm, and stroke risk are addressed.

sub: Rate control in stable atrial fibrillation
text: A hemodynamically stable patient with AF has a resting ventricular rate of 145/min and no pre-excitation. What is the best initial management principle?
options: No treatment because AF is stable
Aspirin as the only rate-control drug
Use an appropriate AV-nodal rate-control agent selected for comorbidities and ventricular function
rationale: Stable AF with rapid ventricular response is commonly managed initially with an AV-nodal rate-control agent. Agent selection must account for ventricular function, blood pressure, conduction disease, and other contraindications.

sub: Resting heart-rate target in atrial fibrillation
text: A patient whose primary diagnosis is AF is treated with rate control and is clinically stable. Which resting heart-rate target reflects CCS guidance?
rationale: CCS recommends titrating rate-control therapy toward a resting heart rate of 100/min or less in patients presenting primarily with AF, while also assessing symptoms and tolerance.

sub: Rhythm control for symptomatic atrial fibrillation
text: A 58-year-old remains markedly exercise-intolerant and dyspneic from AF despite adequate rate control. What is the best next strategy?
options: Discuss a rhythm-control strategy such as cardioversion, antiarrhythmic therapy, or ablation according to patient factors
Accept symptoms permanently because rate control always ends management
Add aspirin solely to restore sinus rhythm
rationale: Persistent AF-related symptoms despite satisfactory rate control support a rhythm-control discussion. The method depends on AF pattern, structural heart disease, risks, preferences, and local expertise.

sub: Elective cardioversion with AF of unknown duration
text: A stable patient with AF of unknown duration is scheduled for elective cardioversion. Which preparation is appropriate?
options: Use at least three weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation before cardioversion, or an accepted imaging-guided strategy
Use aspirin for one hour before cardioversion
Delay anticoagulation until one month afterward
Anticoagulation is unnecessary when symptoms are mild
rationale: AF lasting more than 48 hours or of unknown duration can be associated with left atrial thrombus. Elective cardioversion generally requires therapeutic anticoagulation beforehand or a transesophageal-echo-guided alternative.

text: A stable patient with AF of unknown duration needs earlier cardioversion and has not completed three weeks of anticoagulation. Which alternative is appropriate?
options: Use a chest radiograph to exclude atrial thrombus
Establish therapeutic anticoagulation and perform TEE to exclude left atrial thrombus before cardioversion
Use exercise testing as the thrombus screen
Give dual antiplatelet therapy instead of anticoagulation
rationale: A TEE-guided strategy can permit earlier cardioversion when therapeutic anticoagulation is established and imaging excludes left atrial or appendage thrombus.

text: An unstable patient requires immediate synchronized cardioversion for AF of uncertain duration. What is the best anticoagulation principle?
options: Delay lifesaving cardioversion for three weeks
Initiate therapeutic anticoagulation as soon as possible, ideally before cardioversion when time allows, without delaying stabilization
Anticoagulation depends only on ventricular rate
rationale: Emergency cardioversion should not be delayed when AF is causing instability. Therapeutic anticoagulation should begin as soon as possible, ideally before the shock if the clinical situation permits.

text: A 67-year-old with documented non-valvular AF has no previous stroke and no contraindication to anticoagulation. What is the recommended stroke-prevention strategy?
options: No therapy because no stroke has occurred
Offer oral anticoagulation under the CHADS-65 approach
rationale: The CCS CHADS-65 algorithm recommends oral anticoagulation for most patients with AF who are 65 years or older, even without another CHADS2 factor.

text: A 54-year-old with AF and chronic hypertension has no contraindication to treatment. What is the best stroke-prevention plan?
options: Offer oral anticoagulation because hypertension is a CHADS2 risk factor
Aspirin is always equivalent to anticoagulation
Use anticoagulation only if AF becomes persistent
rationale: Under CHADS-65, a patient younger than 65 with a CHADS2 factor such as hypertension, heart failure, diabetes, or previous stroke/TIA is generally offered oral anticoagulation.

text: A 42-year-old with paroxysmal AF has no heart failure, hypertension, diabetes, previous stroke/TIA, or vascular disease. What is the best routine antithrombotic plan?
options: No routine antithrombotic therapy under the low-risk CHADS-65 pathway
Full-dose anticoagulation for every AF episode
rationale: A patient younger than 65 with no CHADS2 risk factors and no other vascular indication is low risk in the CCS algorithm and generally does not need antithrombotic therapy solely for AF.

sub: DOAC preference in non-valvular atrial fibrillation
text: A patient with non-valvular AF requires oral anticoagulation and has no contraindication to a DOAC. Which agent strategy is preferred for most patients?
options: A DOAC such as apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban, or rivaroxaban rather than warfarin
No therapy if AF is paroxysmal
rationale: Canadian guidance prefers a DOAC over warfarin for most eligible patients with non-valvular AF because efficacy is at least comparable and intracranial bleeding is lower.

text: A patient with AF has a mechanical mitral valve and needs long-term stroke prevention. Which anticoagulant is appropriate?
options: Any DOAC at the lowest dose
A vitamin K antagonist such as warfarin
No therapy if rate is controlled
rationale: Valvular AF is defined by a mechanical heart valve or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis. Vitamin K antagonist therapy is used; DOACs are not the appropriate substitute in this setting.

text: A patient with AF takes warfarin without adverse effects, maintains INR 2.0–3.0, and has time in therapeutic range above 70%. What is a reasonable plan?
rationale: Although DOACs are preferred for most new eligible patients, continuing warfarin is reasonable when INR control is good, time in therapeutic range exceeds 70%, and the patient is doing well.

sub: AF anticoagulation with stable coronary disease
text: A patient with AF takes a DOAC and is three years past PCI with stable coronary disease and no other antiplatelet indication. What is the best long-term plan?
options: Stop the DOAC and use aspirin
Add aspirin routinely to prevent stroke
Continue anticoagulant monotherapy without routine antiplatelet addition
rationale: Beyond one year after PCI or CABG in stable coronary disease, routinely adding an antiplatelet agent to DOAC therapy increases bleeding without significant ischemic benefit.
